ut_hidden_heavenly_slab.blurb: A long, gently tilted slab high in Tanners Gulch, a side drainage of Little Cottonwood Canyon east of Salt Lake City. It holds 22 climbs, nearly all trad and several of them multi-pitch, with one bolted line. Grades start around 5.6 and run to a lone 5.12; the heart of the crag is 5.7 through 5.10, with the 5.10s the most common. The slab stretches beyond 200 feet and steepens into a black-streaked headwall in places, and some climbers liken the feel to City of Rocks. Rock near the base is somewhat broken, and the walk in climbs loose, rubbly ground, so it suits parties comfortable with ground-up style adventure rather than polished cragging.

ut_china_slab.blurb: A wall of lower-angle faces next to the steeper China Cave in Logan Canyon, in northern Utah's Cache Valley. Of its 22 climbs, most are bolted, with a couple of trad lines and one boulder problem at V4. The sport grades lean hard: expect mostly 5.11 through 5.13, with only a few at 5.10 and a single easy line near 5.5, so there is little for someone looking for moderate bolted climbing. The style is technical and sometimes bold face climbing rather than overhanging power. Reaching it takes only a short stroll beside the river from the shared parking.

ut_egg_the.blurb: A speckled, pocketed face in Little Cottonwood Canyon, reached from the lower canyon park-and-ride lot by a switchbacking climbers' trail and a short fourth-class scramble at the base. There are 22 climbs: a trad-leaning mix with a good number of bolted lines and one aid route. Grades run from about 5.5 to 5.12, with plenty in the 5.7 to 5.10 range. The face is nicely angled but the routes run long and feel exposed, and many go in more than one pitch, so plan on a rappel with two ropes or a walk off. It is a warm spot that works as a winter crag.

ut_blue_gramma_cliff.blurb: One of the first big cliffs you meet when driving into Indian Creek in southeast Utah, and a mellow place to get a feel for the desert's crack climbing. All 22 climbs are trad, built on clean sandstone corners, many only about 50 feet tall. Grades cluster in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, with a handful at 5.9 and a single 5.13, so it fits climbers stepping up to Creek-style splitters rather than total beginners. It tends to be quieter than the headline walls farther up the road, which makes it handy for an unhurried introduction or a warm-up day.

ut_trenchtown.blurb: A mostly bolted crag high in the La Sal Mountains above Moab, and the first wall you reach when heading down from the upper parking area at Upper Dakota Crag. Twenty of its 22 climbs are sport and two are trad. The grade spread is friendly to intermediates: a couple of 5.8s and 5.9s, then plenty of 5.10 and 5.11, and a few climbs at 5.12. Routes are on sandstone, and the setting in the aspens at roughly 9,800 feet makes for a very different day than the desert walls below.
ut_trenchtown.approach: From the upper parking area, a trail drops downhill through aspen trees to the first routes in about five minutes.

ut_flytrap_the.blurb: A north-facing sport wall in Crawdad Canyon near Veyo, northeast of St. George, where nearly every route stays shaded through the day, which is a real asset in summer heat. All 22 climbs are bolted. The grades span roughly 5.7 to 5.13, with the 5.10s and 5.11s making up the biggest share, plus several 5.12s. The base is only a short stroll past the swimming area, so it is a convenient and sociable spot, and you may draw an audience from the pool.

ut_theater_the.blurb: A bowl-shaped amphitheater of tall, steep sport climbs along River Road outside Moab, part of the Take-Out Beach cluster of crags. Twenty-one of the 22 routes are bolted and one is trad. Grades start at 5.10 and top out in the 5.12s, with 5.10 and 5.11 the bulk, so it is geared toward solid intermediates and up. It is a sandstone wall, and the exposure to the sun is strong, with heat a serious consideration on warm days. The trail in includes a brief third-class scramble before arriving at the left side of the wall.

ut_gash_the.blurb: A smaller, quieter wall in Indian Creek, southeast Utah, with a handful of well-regarded lines and a good place for ticking off classic crack climbs without the crowds of the larger cliffs. Of its 22 routes, nearly all are trad, with one sport-and-aid line. Grades center on 5.10, which accounts for most of the routes, with a smattering at 5.11 and single climbs at 5.9 and 5.12. The wall mostly faces southeast, gets sun for much of the day in the high season, and sits back in the valley, so it is well sheltered from wind.
